topic: Carbon dioxide and methane as greenhouse gases
subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement about greenhouse gases in the Earth's atmosphere is correct?
items.correct: Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane are all greenhouse gases.
items.misconception: Water vapour is a natural gas and so is not a greenhouse gas.
items.why: Students associate greenhouse gases with pollution from human activity, and water vapour does not feel like a pollutant, so it is dropped from the list. Learn the three named gases as a set: water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane. Being natural does not stop a gas absorbing long wavelength radiation.
items.random_wrong: Only gases released by human activity act as greenhouse gases.

items.q: What do greenhouse gases in the atmosphere do for living things on Earth?
items.correct: They keep temperatures on Earth high enough to support life.
items.misconception: They block the ultraviolet radiation coming from the Sun.
items.why: The greenhouse effect and the hole in the ozone layer are met at the same time and both involve gases high in the atmosphere, so the two stories merge. Ozone depletion and the greenhouse effect are separate: one is about ultraviolet radiation being blocked, the other about long wavelength radiation being absorbed and re-radiated.
items.random_wrong: They supply the oxygen that living organisms need for respiration.

items.q: Which statement best describes the greenhouse effect?
items.correct: Short wavelength radiation passes through; long wavelength is absorbed.
items.misconception: Long wavelength radiation passes through and short wavelength is absorbed.
items.why: The Sun is the obvious source of heat, so students assume the atmosphere must be absorbing sunlight rather than radiation emitted back out by the ground. Track the two steps: short wavelength radiation passes through and warms the surface; the surface then emits long wavelength radiation, which greenhouse gases absorb.
items.random_wrong: Greenhouse gases reflect the incoming radiation back down to the ground.

items.q: Radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the ground. What happens next?
items.correct: The warmed surface emits longer wavelength radiation.
items.misconception: The ground reflects the radiation back at the same wavelength.
items.why: Textbook arrows curving back to the ground look like reflection, and reflection is the easier idea to picture, so absorption and re-radiation are skipped. Use the words the specification uses: the radiation is absorbed by the gas and then re-radiated, not bounced off a surface.
items.random_wrong: The surface emits radiation of an even shorter wavelength.

items.q: What do greenhouse gases do with the long wavelength radiation they absorb?
items.correct: They re-radiate it in all directions, including back towards the Earth.
items.misconception: They reflect all of it straight back down to the Earth's surface.
items.why: Textbook arrows curving back to the ground look like reflection, and reflection is the easier idea to picture, so absorption and re-radiation are skipped. Use the words the specification uses: the radiation is absorbed by the gas and then re-radiated, not bounced off a surface.
items.random_wrong: They store it permanently, so the energy never leaves the gas.

items.q: Which human activity increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
items.correct: Burning fossil fuels in power stations and vehicles.
items.misconception: Growing rice in fields that are kept flooded all year.
items.why: Carbon dioxide dominates the news coverage, so every source gets filed under it and methane sources are never learned separately. Keep two short lists: carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels and deforestation; methane from cattle farming and decay of waste in landfill sites.
items.random_wrong: Keeping large herds of cattle on grassland.

items.q: Explain why cutting down large areas of forest increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the air.
items.correct: Fewer trees are left to remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis.
items.misconception: Trees give out carbon dioxide, so cutting them down helps the air.
items.why: Students remember that plants respire and release carbon dioxide, and forget that over a growing tree's life photosynthesis removes far more than respiration returns. Deforestation raises atmospheric carbon dioxide in two ways: less is removed by photosynthesis, and burning or decay of the felled wood releases more.
items.random_wrong: Cutting the trees down releases the methane that is stored in wood.

items.q: Which pair of human activities both increase the amount of methane in the atmosphere?
items.correct: Cattle farming and rice growing.
items.misconception: Landfill sites and burning of coal.
items.why: Combustion is treated as a single 'pollution' event, so all the gases a student has heard of get attached to it. Match each activity to its gas. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel produces carbon dioxide and water, not methane.
items.random_wrong: Deforestation and cattle farming.

items.q: A student is asked to name two human activities that increase the amount of carbon dioxide. Which pair is correct?
items.correct: Burning fossil fuels for electricity, and deforestation.
items.misconception: Cattle farming, and decay of waste in landfill sites.
items.why: Carbon dioxide dominates the news coverage, so every source gets filed under it and methane sources are never learned separately. Keep two short lists: carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels and deforestation; methane from cattle farming and decay of waste in landfill sites.
items.random_wrong: Burning fossil fuels, and keeping herds of cattle.

items.q: Which statement best describes what scientists say about human activity and the Earth's temperature?
items.correct: Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists expect the Earth's surface to warm.
items.misconception: Scientists have now proved that human activity is the only possible cause of warming.
items.why: 'Proof' is used loosely in everyday speech and in mathematics, so students expect scientific claims to be certain rather than well evidenced. Use the specification's own wording: based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists believe. Evidence can be strong without being called proof.
items.random_wrong: Scientists disagree with each other, so there is no reliable evidence at all.

items.q: Why do different climate models give different predictions for future temperatures?
items.correct: Global climate is a very complex system, so models must be simplified.
items.misconception: Climate models are built on opinion rather than on any real measured data.
items.why: The word 'model' suggests something made up, and students rarely see the measured data a climate model is built from. The specification says complex systems are difficult to model, which leads to simplified models. Simplified is not the same as invented.
items.random_wrong: The temperature of the whole of the atmosphere cannot be measured well.

items.q: A newspaper article about climate change is described as biased. What does this mean?
items.correct: It presents only part of the evidence.
items.misconception: Its thermometers were badly calibrated.
items.why: 'Bias' has a technical meaning in measurement work, and students transfer it to reporting without noticing the change of meaning. In this section bias is about selection and presentation of evidence in the media, not about the accuracy of a thermometer.
items.random_wrong: It quotes peer-reviewed research papers.

items.q: A website claims that the world is cooling, using two years of readings from one weather station. What is the best evaluation of this evidence?
items.correct: The sample is too small and the period too short to show a global trend.
items.misconception: The evidence is strong because real temperatures were measured.
items.why: Students judge evidence by whether it was measured rather than by whether the sample and time span match the claim being made. Evaluate evidence against the claim: a global, long-term claim needs global, long-term data.
items.random_wrong: The evidence is worthless because a website is not a journal.

items.q: Which of these is a genuine uncertainty in the evidence base for global climate change?
items.correct: Future emissions are not known, so predictions are given as a range.
items.misconception: Nobody had measured the temperature of the Earth before the year 2000.
items.why: In everyday speech being uncertain means not knowing, which sounds like incompetence rather than an honest statement of limits. Uncertainty is reported precisely because the work is careful: it states how far predictions may range, and why.
items.random_wrong: Scientists made mistakes when they recorded their measurements.

items.q: Why is peer review of climate research important?
items.correct: Other scientists check the methods and conclusions before publication.
items.misconception: It proves that the conclusions are right and settles the matter for good.
items.why: Peer review is introduced as a quality check, and students round 'checked' up to 'certain'. Peer review raises confidence and filters out poor work; later evidence can still change the conclusion.
items.random_wrong: It lets the general public vote on which scientific results to believe.

items.q: Why is a rise of about one degree in the average global temperature important?
items.correct: It shifts the climate of the whole Earth.
items.misconception: Every place on Earth is now one degree warmer.
items.why: Students compare the average with the day-to-day range they experience, which is much bigger, and conclude the rise is trivial. A shift in the global average moves the whole distribution, which changes ice cover, sea level and the frequency of extreme weather.
items.random_wrong: It is too small to change the weather at all.

items.q: Which of these is a potential effect of global climate change?
items.correct: Sea level rise, causing flooding of low-lying land.
items.misconception: More acid rain falling on lakes and forests.
items.why: All the atmospheric pollution topics are taught close together, so their effects get pooled into one list. Keep the effects of climate change separate: sea level rise, flooding, extreme weather, changed rainfall patterns and changes to species distribution.
items.random_wrong: A larger hole in the ozone layer each spring.

items.q: Which list contains only potential effects of global climate change?
items.correct: Flooding, more extreme weather, changes to species distribution.
items.misconception: Flooding, deforestation, more frequent storms and stronger winds.
items.why: Causes and effects appear in the same paragraph of most revision notes, and melting ice is the image most strongly linked to the topic. Sort the topic into causes (human activities releasing carbon dioxide and methane) and effects (sea level rise, flooding, extreme weather, species changes).
items.random_wrong: Rising sea level, acid rain, changes to rainfall patterns.

items.q: A report says that the risk to a coastal city from climate change is high. What does describing the risk involve?
items.correct: How likely the flooding is, and how severe it would be.
items.misconception: Only how many years it will be before the flooding happens.
items.why: Students compare the average with the day-to-day range they experience, which is much bigger, and conclude the rise is trivial. A shift in the global average moves the whole distribution, which changes ice cover, sea level and the frequency of extreme weather.
items.random_wrong: Only how many people believe that the report is correct.

items.q: What is the carbon footprint of a product?
items.correct: Greenhouse gases emitted over its full life cycle.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide given off while the product is made.
items.why: Manufacture is the stage students picture first, and 'full life cycle' is easy to read past in the definition. Include every stage: raw materials, manufacture, transport, use and disposal, and include methane as well as carbon dioxide.
items.random_wrong: The mass of carbon that the finished object contains.

items.q: Which statement about a carbon footprint is correct?
items.correct: It includes methane as well as carbon dioxide, at every stage.
items.misconception: It counts carbon dioxide only, from the factory stage.
items.why: Manufacture is the stage students picture first, and 'full life cycle' is easy to read past in the definition. Include every stage: raw materials, manufacture, transport, use and disposal, and include methane as well as carbon dioxide.
items.random_wrong: It is the carbon locked inside the finished product.

items.q: A company wants to reduce the carbon footprint of its factory. Which action would do this?
items.correct: Take the factory's electricity from wind and solar farms.
items.misconception: Fit filters to the chimneys to trap all the carbon dioxide.
items.why: Flue gas desulfurisation is taught nearby, so the same fix is assumed to work for every gas leaving a chimney. Carbon dioxide is a product of combustion itself, so it is reduced by burning less fuel, switching fuel or capturing and storing the gas.
items.random_wrong: Measure the carbon dioxide released at every stage.

items.q: Which action would reduce emissions of methane?
items.correct: Collect the gas from landfill sites and burn it as a fuel.
items.misconception: Bury much more waste in landfill so that the gas cannot escape.
items.why: Combustion is treated as a single 'pollution' event, so all the gases a student has heard of get attached to it. Match each activity to its gas. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel produces carbon dioxide and water, not methane.
items.random_wrong: Fit filters to the power station chimneys to trap the methane.

items.q: Give one reason why actions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions may be limited.
items.correct: Alternative technologies cost a lot.
items.misconception: There is no evidence for the warming.
items.why: Media framing of the topic as an unsettled argument is carried over into the reasons why action is slow. Give practical reasons: cost, the pace of scientific and technological development, lack of international agreement, and lack of public information.
items.random_wrong: Emissions cannot be measured at all today.

items.q: Would the Earth be better off with no greenhouse gases at all?
items.correct: No. Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere maintain temperatures on Earth high enough to support life; the concern is the extra amount added by human activity.
items.misconception: The greenhouse effect is simply pollution, so removing all greenhouse gases would be good.
items.why: The word 'greenhouse' is almost always met in news reports about global warming, so it becomes attached to harm, and the natural effect that keeps the Earth warm enough to live on is never met. Separate the natural greenhouse effect, which supports life, from the enhanced effect caused by rising amounts of carbon dioxide and methane.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do greenhouse gases make up most of the atmosphere?
items.correct: No. Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99% of the air; the greenhouse gases are present in much smaller amounts.
items.misconception: A gas can only have a large warming effect if there is a large amount of it in the air.
items.why: Students reason that a big effect needs a big cause, and are rarely shown how small the carbon dioxide and methane fractions of the atmosphere actually are. A small amount of gas can have a large effect because each molecule absorbs long wavelength radiation; amount and effect are not proportional in a simple way.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the atmosphere trap warm air like a blanket?
items.correct: No. The greenhouse effect is about radiation being absorbed and re-radiated, not about warm air being physically held in.
items.misconception: Greenhouse gases stop hot air escaping, the way a blanket or a glass greenhouse does.
items.why: The greenhouse analogy is taught first and taken literally; a real greenhouse works mainly by stopping convection, which is a different mechanism. Describe the effect in terms of radiation: short wavelength in, long wavelength absorbed and re-radiated. The blanket picture explains the wrong mechanism.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If scientists disagree about details, is the evidence worthless?
items.correct: No. Disagreement about the size and timing of effects sits alongside a large body of peer-reviewed evidence that the surface temperature is rising.
items.misconception: Because some scientists disagree, nothing about climate change can be relied on.
items.why: Media coverage stages the topic as a two-sided debate, which makes uncertainty about detail look like uncertainty about everything. Distinguish the well-evidenced core from the uncertain detail; uncertainty in predictions is normal in a complex system.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the carbon footprint the mass of carbon inside the product?
items.correct: No. It is an amount of greenhouse gas emitted, not carbon contained in the object.
items.misconception: A product's carbon footprint is the amount of carbon it is made of.
items.why: The word 'carbon' in the name points at the material, and 'footprint' is a vague enough word to let that reading stand. Read the definition as written: the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.9.2 Carbon dioxide and methane as greenhouse gases
